blocks.html: The saying of the Philosopher, renewed in our laws, is that for our affirming or denying, the truth changes not at all a2; which, as Cicero says in a certain place, has always had such power that by any art, device or contrivance of man whatsoever it has never been able to be overturned; and though it have no protector to take up its defence, it defends itself well enough of itself b2. And in another place: O how great, says he, is the force of truth, which against the wit, ruses and wiles of man defends itself easily, without the help or succour of any other c2.

notes.citation: Digest 50.1 (Ad municipalem et de incolis), l. Adsumptio (D. 50.1.6 pr., Ulpian)
notes.gloss: Adsumptio originis, quae non est, veritati non praeiudicat — "the assumption of an origin one does not have does not prejudice the truth: for no one by lying makes himself of no origin, nor by claiming another's origin acquires it."

notes.citation: Cicero, In Vatinium as cited — the sentence on the power of truth is not in the speech as it survives (the word veritas does not occur in it); unidentified, cf. Pro Caelio 63, cited next
notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon con tre vatin.
notes.gloss: Coras's paraphrase — truth never overturned by human art, and defending itself without a protector — is close to the Pro Caelio passage cited next; whether he has a distinct In Vatinium sentence in mind could not be confirmed.

notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon pro M. Cœlio.
notes.gloss: O magnam vim veritatis, quae contra hominum ingenia, calliditatem, sollertiam contraque fictas omnium insidias facile se per se ipsa defendat! — "O great power of truth, which against the wit, cunning and cleverness of men, and against the feigned snares of all, easily defends itself by itself."
